claims.text: Progressive plastic deformation under sustained loading in FCC/BCC high-entropy-alloy nanoscale multilayers is governed by the interplay between dislocation activity and nanoscale interface order.
Short-range order and interface coherency modulate dislocation mobility and accumulation.
Changes in dislocation mobility and accumulation caused by interface structure control the creep rate and deformation pattern.
Controlled deposition can produce multilayers with uniform layer thickness, minimal residual stress, and an intermediate degree of interface order.
Changing annealing or deposition protocols can systematically vary short-range order and interface coherency while layer thickness and overall composition remain constant.
Interface short-range order and coherency can act as obstacles or channels for dislocation motion.
Under sustained loading, dislocations nucleate and accumulate at FCC/BCC interfaces.
Enhanced interface order temporarily impedes dislocation movement.
Temporary impediment of dislocations by enhanced interface order produces initial creep resistance followed by localized slip events.
Reduced interface order lowers barriers to dislocation motion.
Lower dislocation barriers at reduced-order interfaces produce a more uniform but higher creep rate.
Relative to an intermediate-order baseline, enhanced-order samples will have lower initial creep rates.
Enhanced-order samples will exhibit sudden localized slip events after a threshold strain.
Relative to the baseline, reduced-order samples will exhibit a higher and more uniform creep rate.
The proposed behavior is limited to conditions in which the nanoscale multilayer architecture remains intact and dislocation-based deformation dominates over extensive diffusion or recrystallization.
